content:
**Subject and central claims.** This section opens a chapter on vision, arguing that perception solves "ill-posed" inverse problems — retinal data underdetermine the world, since an ellipse could be an oval seen head-on or a circle slanted, and gray could be shaded snow or sunlit coal. Vision becomes solvable by adding premises about how the world is on average: matter is cohesive, surfaces are uniformly colored, objects do not line up confusingly. When the environment matches the ancestral average we see truly; when assumptions are violated we fall for illusions, which is why psychologists study them — illusions unmask the installed assumptions (file page 127). Perception is described as the consistently adaptation-minded branch of psychology: its job is reverse-engineering true forms and materials, because knowing where food, predators, and cliffs are has obvious survival value (file page 127).

**Representation and compositionality.** Citing David Marr, Pinker presents vision as producing "from images of the external world a description that is useful to the viewer and not cluttered with irrelevant information" (file page 127). This description is not spoken English but an internal abstract code ("mentalese"): we call a book "rectangular" though it projects a trapezoid, grasp it with a rectangular posture, build rectangular shelves, and infer it fits rectangular gaps (file page 127). The symbol "rectangle" and propositions like "book lying face down on shelf near door" are the description Marr meant (file page 127). Pinker's reasoning: without a shared description, language, walking, grasping, planning, and imagining would each need to re-derive that a trapezoid is a rectangle — implausible, since naming a slanted rectangle transfers to holding and fitting it. Vision writes an object-based, three-dimensional representation "on a blackboard readable by all the mental modules," though some fast motor channels siphon information separately (file page 127). This is the section's clearest statement of a compositional, modality-general representation.

**Perception mechanisms and examples.** Autostereograms exploit four tricks, beginning with pictures themselves: projection loses distance (a photon's ray extends to infinity), so any retinal image matches infinitely many 3-D arrangements (file pages 128–129). Ames's peep-show rooms align irregular matter into regular projections; the brain "hates coincidences," so a slanted wall with crooked angles projects a rectangle and a child appears to tower over a parent (file page 128). Leonardo's window explains painting: copy contours from a fixed vantage and the viewer's eye receives the same rays (file page 129). Previewed assumptions include uniform surface color and texture, regular parallel or right-angled figures, and compact silhouettes (occlusion: a bite filled by another object means the first is behind) (file page 129). Paintings are only partly illusory; we use canvas and frame to compensate for vantage, imperfectly (front-row movies warp) (file page 129).

**Depth, time, and causation cues.** Binocular parallax yields stereoscopic depth via trigonometry on the disparity between the eyes' views, gaze angle, and eye separation — discovered by Charles Wheatstone in 1838, not by Leonardo (file pages 129–130). Monocular cues persist with one eye: tapering, occlusion, ground placement, texture gradients, and above all motion — optical flow from moving vantage gives depth (file page 130). The brain is "an opportunistic and mathematically adroit consumer of information" (file page 131). Wheatstone's stereoscope works only if the brain assumes both eyes view one world; but the focusing reflex (lens accommodation) and convergence reflex are coupled, so naive stereoscopes blur or double images. Stereo gives relative depth only; eye-position feedback anchors absolute depth (file page 131).

**Limits and disagreements.** Pinker notes social-science folklore treated emotions as culturally relative; Paul Ekman's New Guinea work countered this, though the deeper point is that photographed expressions are seen as depictions at all (file page 128). The section is descriptive, not a learning theory: assumptions are attributed to natural selection, not to individual learning.

**Engineering implications (mine, not Pinker's).** A thinking machine could implement an inverse-graphics stage that resolves ambiguity by explicit priors (cohesion, uniform reflectance, non-coincidence), publishing object-centered 3-D propositions to a shared workspace for language, planning, and motor modules — matching the "blackboard" idea (file page 127). Disparity plus vergence state gives relative and absolute depth (file pages 130–131); optical flow supplies time-varying structure (file page 130). Illusions become diagnostic tests for priors. The section leaves unsolved how symbols acquire meaning, how priors are learned or revised, and how goals, memory, analogy, or creativity operate; those require further sources. Nothing here demonstrates consciousness or general intelligence.
